Say whether one list equals another, sits inside it, contains it, or none of these.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/sublist) (MIT). Listed under [Collections & Algorithms](/examples/?subject=collections-and-algorithms).

```nomi-run
// FILE: sublist.nomi
//# How two lists relate: equal, one inside the other, or neither.

/// How the first list relates to the second.
pub enum Relation {
    Equal
    Sublist
    Superlist
    Unequal
}

/// How `first` relates to `second`. One list is inside another when its
/// elements appear there in order and next to each other.
pub fn sublist<T>(first: List<T>, second: List<T>) -> Relation where T: Equatable {
    case {
        first == second -> .Equal
        contains_run(second, first) -> .Sublist
        contains_run(first, second) -> .Superlist
        _ -> .Unequal
    }
}

/// Whether `run` appears in `list` with its elements next to each other.
/// Every list holds the empty run; `Iter.windows` of size 0 yields nothing.
fn contains_run<T>(list: List<T>, run: List<T>) -> Bool where T: Equatable {
    Iter.is_empty(run) or Iter.windows(list, Iter.count(run)) |> Iter.any(&(&1 == run))
}

// FILE: sublist_test.nomi
import sublist.{self, Relation}

test "sublist" {
    cases = [
        #("empty lists", [], [], Relation.Equal),
        #("empty list within non empty list", [], [1, 2, 3], .Sublist),
        #("non empty list contains empty list", [1, 2, 3], [], .Superlist),
        #("list equals itself", [1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], .Equal),
        #("different lists", [1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4], .Unequal),
        #("false start", [1, 2, 5], [0, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 5, 6], .Sublist),
        #("consecutive", [1, 1, 2], [0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2], .Sublist),
        #("sublist at start", [0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], .Sublist),
        #("sublist in middle", [2, 3, 4], [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], .Sublist),
        #("sublist at end", [3, 4, 5], [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], .Sublist),
        #("at start of superlist", [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [0, 1, 2], .Superlist),
        #("in middle of superlist", [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [2, 3], .Superlist),
        #("at end of superlist", [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [3, 4, 5], .Superlist),
        #("first list missing element from second list", [1, 3], [1, 2, 3], .Unequal),
        #("second list missing element from first list", [1, 2, 3], [1, 3], .Unequal),
        #("first list missing additional digits from second list", [1, 2], [1, 22], .Unequal),
        #("order matters to a list", [1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1], .Unequal),
        #("same digits but different numbers", [1, 0, 1], [10, 1], .Unequal),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, first, second, expected), description {
        assert sublist.sublist(first, second) == expected
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- The answer is a `Relation` enum of the four outcomes, not a string.
- `sublist` is generic over any `Equatable` element, though the canonical cases are all `Int`s.
- The three checks are arms of a `case` with no subject, in the order the outcomes are tested: equal first, since equal lists also contain each other.
- `contains_run` asks whether any of the longer list's `Iter.windows` of the run's length equals the run, after answering the empty run itself, since a window of size 0 does not exist. The other way is to walk the longer list with a list pattern and ask `List.starts_with(rest, run)` at each position, which needs no lengths.
- The 18 canonical cases are one `subtests` table. The first row's `[]` and `[]` take their element type from the later rows.
